title: What is the perimeter of the snowflake at any step?
description: The video takes the number of sides at Step n and the length of each side, and multiplies them to get the perimeter of the snowflake of {{NAME_3}}. It checks the result at Step one and Step two and says what happens as the steps go on.
teaching_notes: One idea: the perimeter is the number of sides times the length of one side, and each step multiplies it by four thirds. Watch for students who think the perimeter stays three units because the shape looks the same size.

video_script.why: The child finds the perimeter the way the example in the book does, by multiplying the number of sides by the length of one side, and then writes it for any step.
video_script.substitution: Multiply the sides at Step n by the length of each side at Step n.
video_script.anchor: the snowflake of {{NAME_3}} in the book, starting from an equilateral triangle with each side one unit long
video_script.payoff_line: At Step n the perimeter is three times, four thirds all to the power n, units

final_answer.value: 3 x (4/3) to the power n units; the perimeter keeps growing
final_answer.spoken: three times, four thirds all to the power n, units, and the perimeter keeps growing

names.{{NAME_3}}: Swedish mathematician who described the snowflake in 1904

hold_back: Answer: 3 x (4/3) to the power n units; the perimeter keeps growing
never_show: perimeter 3 marked as right at Step n
maths_rules: sides at Step n: 3 x (4 to the power n)
each step makes every side one third as long, so each side at Step n is 1 / (3 to the power n)
each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3: 3, 4, 16/3
Step n: 3 x (4/3) to the power n
video_script.design: A table of steps, sides, length of a side and perimeter grows one row at a time; the rule for Step n is written at the bottom.

<bookmark mark='start'/>The starting triangle has each side one unit long.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the perimeter of the shape at Step n?

beats.on_screen: the frames stay on the board with the question mark underlined

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one side cut into 3 equal parts with a bump on the middle part; the 4 new pieces are each marked one third of the old side

marks.four: the four pieces are each marked one third of the old side
marks.rule: the words 4 times as many sides, each a third as long are written

narration: <bookmark mark='bump'/>Every side gets a bump, as in the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='four'/>One side becomes four sides, and each is one third as long.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The sides are four times as many, and each side is a third as long.

beats.on_screen: Given: starting side 1 unit. Each step makes 4 times as many sides, each one third as long.

marks.given: the starting side and the rule are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the starting side is one unit. Each step makes four times as many sides, and each is one third as long.

beats.on_screen: To find: perimeter at Step n

marks.find: the words perimeter at Step n are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the perimeter at Step n.

beats.on_screen: Sides at Step n = 3 x (4 to the power n)

marks.rule: the line each step multiplies the sides by 4 is written
marks.sides: 3 x (4 to the power n) is written in the sides column

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>First, count the sides at Step n. Each step multiplies the sides by four.
<bookmark mark='sides'/>Step n has three times four to the power n sides.

beats.on_screen: Length of one side: Step 1 is 1/3, Step 2 is 1/9, Step n is 1 / (3 to the power n)

marks.rule: the line each step makes every side 1/3 as long is written
marks.length: 1/3, 1/9 and 1 / (3 to the power n) are written in the length column

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Second, find the length of each side. Each step makes every side one third as long.
<bookmark mark='length'/>The sides are one third, then one ninth. At Step n, each side is one over three to the power n.

beats.on_screen: Perimeter = sides x length. Step 1: 12 x 1/3 = 4. Step 2: 48 x 1/9 = 16/3.

marks.one: 12 x 1/3 = 4 is written in the perimeter column
marks.two: 48 x 1/9 = 16/3 is written in the perimeter column

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Third, multiply the number of sides by the length of one side. At Step one, twelve times one third is four.
<bookmark mark='two'/>At Step two, forty eight times one ninth is sixteen over three.

beats.on_screen: Perimeter: 3, 4, 16/3, ... Each step multiplies by 4/3. Step n: 3 x (4/3) to the power n

marks.list: the perimeters 3, 4 and 16/3 are written with arrows marked times 4/3
marks.power: 3 x (4/3) to the power n is written in the Step n row

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Fourth, find the pattern. The perimeters go three, four, sixteen over three. Each step multiplies by four thirds.
<bookmark mark='power'/>After n steps, the perimeter is three times, four thirds all to the power n.

beats.on_screen: Check: n = 1: 3 x 4/3 = 4. n = 2: 3 x 16/9 = 16/3. Both match the table.

marks.one: 3 x 4/3 = 4 is written and ticked against the table
marks.two: 3 x 16/9 = 16/3 is written and ticked against the table

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Fifth, put the steps back in the rule. For n equal to one, three times four thirds is four.
<bookmark mark='two'/>For n equal to two, three times sixteen over nine is sixteen over three. Both match the table.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 3 x (4/3) to the power n units; the perimeter keeps growing

marks.grow: an arrow points up beside the box

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>At Step n the perimeter is three times, four thirds all to the power n, units.
<bookmark mark='grow'/>It keeps growing, because four thirds is more than one.
